segments.text: PI ZONOOZ: Cool.
Well, I'm going to take us out of tech world for a second
and just talk about something that everybody in this room
interacts with, which is healthcare.
We have a massive problem in healthcare,
not just in this country, but across the world.
There's a major capacity issue.
There's not enough clinicians, not enough
trained staff to actually see and treat everybody
on planet Earth.
Just in this country alone, the spending that we do
on administrative tasks-- so the things that are not aligned
to actually delivering care between a clinician
or a patient--
is about 25% representing about $600 billion to $1 trillion
just in the US.
This is a massive problem, and we
think AI and specifically, agents, are the best
suited solution we have to solve and address
this massive inflation in healthcare costs.
And healthcare has changed a lot.
If we think about what healthcare
was maybe 50 or 60 years ago, right.
It was a single one to one relationship between a doctor
and their patient.
Well, healthcare has evolved.
Care pathways have changed.
There's so much information and complexity
in treating every single human being
due to their unique lifestyle, their genetics.
And then you also have to combine that with billing
systems on the back end.
You have to do adequate coding.
You have to get the right authorizations from a payer.
There's a million-and-one tasks that an individual or a system
needs to do in order to provide care.
That's not necessarily the diagnostic relationship
between, again, the patient and the clinician.
And this is what Nimblemind is addressing first.
How do we optimize that and build quality workflows that
can automate those tasks and free up hours for clinicians
to spend more time with their patients?
Now, to do this, it's not simple.
A lot of folks have of implemented copilots and brought
LLMs into these types of workflows,
but it's missing three key ingredients.
You need to be able to do predictable, structured,
consistent tasks.
You need to enable humans in the loop in a systematic way.
And expose low confidence decisions
to experts when appropriate.
And then you need to build objective-driven workflows.
And there's many of these in healthcare.
It's very complex.
So this is, the secret sauce that Nimblemind is addressing.
We're pulling all these three things together
and automating what we call end-to-end healthcare knowledge
work.
So we find the relevant information
across all the myriad systems that exist in a provider.
We understand the context and exceptions.
We complete the multi-step workflow
and highlight things that might need a human in the loop.
And then we return a traceable output to the user.
And the way we do this is with specialty specific models.
I was talking to Matt White in the green room
before coming out here.
He was on stage maybe three or four sessions ago
from the Linux Foundation.
And him and I agree, where these small scale
domain-specific models are the path forward.
And that's what we're doing.
We're training and building our own models
that align to how healthcare is practiced today,
which is specialties.
So we have models that work on oncology, on pathology,
on radiology, nephrology, and a whole long list of others
that aren't on the slide.
And by combining these models together and building
a system of experts, we're able to do high-quality, consistent,
durable tasks in healthcare that can win confidence of clinicians
and drive the right outcomes for patients.
Well, what's one example of this?
Well, we recently published a paper with SingHealth.
I'll be presenting this on October 8 at the conference
here in San Francisco.
We're working with pathology reports.
So what SingHealth wanted to do was
look at over 2 million different pathology reports
and find missed cases of H pylori and gastritis.
Now, if a human were to do this, they'd spend something around
like 82 hours per 1,000 reports.
You can do the math of how that would scale up
to 2 million reports.
We were able to save them over 99% of the time,
and do it at an accuracy that was well
above the threshold for their internal teams
and acceptability.
And to highlight again, the cases where
we needed human intervention.
We were able to do this in less than a week.
The product is live.
We're about 2 and 1/2 years old.
We're venture backed.
I didn't want to risk it with a video.
So these are just going to be still shots of the product.
But you can go on and sign up.
We build a lot of scalable APIs that you can integrate with.
We kind of white label our product
to a lot of different health tech companies
that are in the market today.
And something that I'm very excited about
is we also have a new feature where you can orchestrate
and build your own workflows.
So a lot of our maybe not so technical users and providers
are building and designing their own workflows
and going live with them in our model framework
that's safe and consistent and effective for the healthcare
setting.
We've got about 100 different customers
that we work with around the world.
Some of our research partners and customers are listed here.
I won't go through them, but some of the world's
top institutions in the AMC or medical space.
I invite you to read our papers were published and presented
at NeurIPS, at ML4H.
And recently, we're going to present at DAIHN.
And we recently presented at [? Sailor's ?] [? Way ?]
as well.
All of our papers are available for you to read.
If you're interested in healthcare,
I invite you to take a look at those.
And just a quick background on me
for the investors in the room.
I came from AWS and stripe.
I helped launch over 40 different products,
including Alexa for healthcare and the first epic
deployment on AWS.
My co-founder Navin Kumar, who's our chief AI officer,
has a PhD from Yale and was the data science lead
at New York City's Health and Hospital Systems.
Thank you for the time.
Appreciate you all.
Cheers.
